ERROR_ANALYSIS_TEXT: On BDG2 the Spearman correlation between per-building coverage and CV(RMSE) is -0.65 for CQR and -0.36 for HSC-CQR (-0.96 for SCP-stage), i.e. HSC weakens the dependence of reliability on forecast difficulty. Across usage classes with at least 30 building × seed units, the largest reduction of the absolute coverage deviation is observed for 'Education' and the smallest for 'Lodging/residential' (Fig. [-@fig:errors]b). Of the 1265 building × seed units, 43 remain under-covered by HSC-CQR. Their median within-window level change |log(mean load weeks 5–8 / weeks 1–4)| is 0.197 versus 0.053 for the others (Mann–Whitney p < 0.001); remaining failures are therefore associated with regime changes during onboarding. Their first-week volatility is 0.118 versus 0.113 (p = 0.725). On UCI, 3 of 475 units remain under-covered; the corresponding level-change medians are 0.838 versus 0.049 (p < 0.001).
ABSTRACT: Demand response, flexibility bidding and measurement-and-verification need day-ahead prediction intervals for individual buildings, often from the first days after a building is metered. Interval methods are usually judged by coverage pooled over many buildings, which can hide buildings whose intervals are systematically too narrow. We evaluate per-building interval reliability during onboarding under a pre-registered, building- and period-disjoint protocol on 842 buildings at 10 sites (Building Data Genome 2) and 315 Portuguese electricity clients, with five seeds, unseen sites, cross-country transfer and stress tests. Using one global forecaster, we compare pooled split conformal prediction, conformalised quantile regression (CQR), group-wise, self-only, adaptive (ACI), temporal-quantile-adjustment and hierarchical calibration, quantile shrinkage, and a pseudo-count shrinkage of the nonconformity-score distribution towards each building's own accumulating scores, with the pseudo-count selected by leave-one-building-out. Pooled CQR left 18.7% (BDG2) and 9.5% (UCI) of new buildings with coverage more than five points below the 90 % target. Score-distribution shrinkage was the most reliable strategy, reducing these shares to 3.4% and 0.6% and the mean absolute coverage deviation from 0.038 to 0.018 (BDG2) at an essentially unchanged interval score; it also improved intervals from a neural quantile model. Similarity-weighted priors and onboarding-stage matching added nothing, leaving a one-parameter layer whose pseudo-count of one to two weeks of hourly scores costs 0.437 ms per building-day.
